title: U.S. House · Mississippi's 1st District
area: Northeast Mississippi, including Tupelo, Corinth, Oxford, and the Golden Triangle area

context.text: Trent Kelly ran unopposed in the March 10, 2026 Republican primary. Cliff Johnson defeated Kelvin Buck in the Democratic primary, 63.4% to 36.6%.

candidates.name: Trent Kelly
candidates.ballotNote: Ran unopposed in the March 10, 2026 Republican primary

summary.text: Trent Kelly is the incumbent Republican U.S. Representative for Mississippi's 1st District, elected in a 2015 special election. A Mississippi attorney and former district attorney, he served 39 years in the Mississippi Army National Guard, retiring as a Major General in April 2025. He sits on the Agriculture, Intelligence and Armed Services committees.

background.text: Born March 1, 1966, in Union, Mississippi; graduated from Union High School and East Central Community College.
Earned a bachelor's degree and a law degree from the University of Mississippi and, in 2010, a master's degree in Strategic Studies from the U.S. Army War College.

Served 39 years in the Mississippi Army National Guard as a combat engineer, beginning in 1985; mobilized for Desert Storm in 1990, deployed to Iraq in 2005 and again in 2009-2010 as a battalion commander, and retired as a Major General in April 2025. Decorations include two Bronze Stars and the Combat Action Badge.
Before Congress, worked as a department store manager and in private law practice in Saltillo, and served as Tupelo city prosecutor (1999-2011).
Served as district attorney for Mississippi's 1st Judicial District from 2012 to 2015, handling felony cases in seven north Mississippi counties.
Won the 2015 special election to succeed Rep. Alan Nunnelee, taking 70% of the vote against Democrat Walter Zinn in the May 12, 2015 runoff.
In the 119th Congress (2025-2026) sits on the Agriculture, Intelligence (Permanent Select) and Armed Services committees, and chairs the Armed Services Subcommittee on Seapower and Projection Forces.
Was unopposed in the March 10, 2026 Republican primary.
According to his congressional website, lives in Saltillo with his wife, Sheila, and their three children, and is a member of Saltillo First United Methodist Church.

priorities.text: Says the federal government's primary role is to keep the United States safe from threats at home and abroad.
Cites agriculture, which he says contributes $7.9 billion to the Mississippi economy, as a top priority through his seat on the House Agriculture Committee.
Says regulations from Washington have increased costs for businesses and wants to reduce that burden.

positions.summary: States on his issues page that the Second Amendment 'is not up for debate' and opposes restricting the rights of legal gun owners.

record.text: Serves on the House Committee on Agriculture, House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, and House Armed Services Committee (chair, Seapower and Projection Forces subcommittee) in the 119th Congress.

candidates.name: Cliff Johnson
candidates.currentRole: Civil rights lawyer and law professor

summary.text: Cliff Johnson is the Democratic nominee for Mississippi's 1st District. A civil rights lawyer and former federal prosecutor, he directs the MacArthur Justice Center at the University of Mississippi School of Law and teaches there. He describes his campaign as focused on working people, democracy and independence from party.

background.text: Earned a B.A. in political science from Mississippi College (1989) and a J.D. from Columbia Law School (1992).
After a federal clerkship, worked three years as an associate at the Jackson law firm Butler Snow, then five years as an Assistant U.S. Attorney.
Was a partner for 13 years at the Jackson firm Pigott & Johnson, then joined the Mississippi Center for Justice.
Was a Fulbright Scholar at the Raoul Wallenberg Institute in Lund, Sweden, in 2005-2006.

Directs the MacArthur Justice Center at the University of Mississippi School of Law, where it has litigated cases on cash bail, debtors' prisons and appointed counsel for indigent defendants, and supervises students in its clinic.
Was named a Public Justice National Trial Lawyer of the Year in 2016 and Mississippi Trial Lawyer of the Year for 2017-18 by the Mississippi Association for Justice.
Describes himself as a lawyer who has practiced in Mississippi for 33 years and as a lifelong Democrat.
Won the March 10, 2026 Democratic primary with 63.4% of the vote over Kelvin Buck.

priorities.text: "Working People Matter": says flat wages and rising prices for groceries, housing and health care are squeezing North Mississippi families while tax cuts go to the wealthy.
priorities.quote: Working People Matter! Too many people in North Mississippi are struggling to make ends meet, and politicians aren't doing enough to make things easier.

priorities.text: "Democracy Matters": says the politicization of the military, attacks on the judiciary, and dismantling of government agencies threaten checks and balances.
"Independence Matters": describes himself as a lifelong Democrat dedicated to Mississippians rather than to a political party.

positions.summary: Candidate Connection survey says he is passionate about health-care policy, citing unaffordable insurance and Mississippians losing Medicaid and ACA coverage.
Criticizes the Trump administration and its supporters for focusing on tax cuts for 'the super-rich' while wages remain flat.

summary.text: Johnny Baucom is the Libertarian candidate for Mississippi's 1st District. He describes himself as a Mississippian raised by a single mother who earned a GED through the National Guard Youth Challenge Program, served in the Army National Guard from 2014 to 2020, and later managed mechanic shops. Ballotpedia lists his profession as environmental specialist.

background.text: Describes himself as raised by a single mother in poverty, and says he left high school after ninth grade.
Says he earned his GED through the National Guard Youth Challenge Program at Camp Shelby in Hattiesburg.
Served in the U.S. Army National Guard from 2014 to 2020 (a six-year contract, per his survey).
Says he used skills from the military to manage multiple mechanic shops; Ballotpedia lists his profession as environmental specialist.
